summary.title: Systems that defy detailed understanding
summary.one_liner: Some complex systems (distributed systems, big balls of mud, client-side JavaScript, deep learning) are better managed by resilience design, statistics and empirical experiments than by tracing every behavior in detail.
keywords: when not to debug root cause
will larson big balls of mud
takeaways: In distributed systems, prefer making the system as a whole resilient (retries, timeouts, fallbacks) over tracing every root cause of a component failure.
Big balls of mud lack comprehensible invariants, so ask questions of the running system with logs, metrics and instrumentation rather than reasoning from source.
Client-side JavaScript errors are best handled statistically: group them, investigate only trends above a rate, and roll out deploys gradually.
For deep learning, use small incremental changes from a working baseline and heavily verify your data pipeline before blaming the model.
Hold both mindsets: theoretical understanding guides experiments, and observations refine mental models.
summary.summary: The post is a follow-up to an essay on understanding computer systems, and it lists four classes of systems where deep, detailed understanding was impractical. These are complex distributed systems, big balls of mud, client-side JavaScript error reporting, and deep learning. For each, the author describes why tracing behavior in detail is hard, such as large dependency stacks, concurrency and message ordering, heterogeneous browser environments, or the lack of comprehensible system logic. The author then describes what works instead, typically systems-level resilience, empirical instrumentation and observability, statistical analysis of error rates, and incremental experimentation. The post closes by arguing that engineers should master and switch between both the understanding-driven and the empirical mindsets.
